abstract.p: The purpose of this study is to construct a mortality model that reasonably explains survival curves and mortality rates in terms of the decline in biological function, which is the phenomenon of ageing. In this model, an individual organism is regarded as a collection of subsystems, and for each subsystem, the model defines human mortality by introducing positive self-repair mechanisms and stochastically generated negative external shocks. The probability density function of the time of death is derived explicitly, and the model parameters are estimated using life tables from Japan and the UK, which demonstrate the existence of multiple parameter sets that fit well with the observed data.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: While individual human death may seem unpredictable from a personal perspective, it can be viewed as a phenomenon governed by some underlying laws when observed at the population level. Life tables, which represent mortality rates and life expectancies, are tabular summaries of this collective phenomenon for countries or specific regions, categorised by age groups and sex. They are not only useful for calculating insurance premiums and formulating social security systems and economic policies, but also for exploring the essence of ageing, lifespan, and investigating whether there exist limitations to human lifespan.

Attempts to mathematically represent life tables using age as a mathematical function have long been made. Examples of such models include the Gompertz model (Gompertz 1825), the Logistic model, and the Kannisto model (Kannisto 1994). In particular, the Gompertz model, which describes an exponential increase in the mortality rate with age, accurately represents the mortality situation with a small number of parameters and is still used for complementing life tables in some countries, even after approximately 200 years since its discovery. The models based on these mathematical functions have shown good fitting with life tables, but their functional forms are derived from empirical observations, and the mechanisms behind their derivation remain unclear. Therefore, various models have been proposed to derive the mortality rate from a physical approach as an attempt to support this phenomenon.

The early representative model by Sacher and Trueco (1962) associated Gompertz’s law with stochastic and constant influences of forces. Additionally, Strehler and Mildvan (1960) derived an exponential increase in mortality rate from the perspective of environmental stress that drives organisms to death and their ability to counteract it, establishing the relationship between parameters of the Gompertz model, known today as the Strehler-Mildvan correlation. Subsequently, the avalanche model by Gavrilov and Gavrilova (1991) and the model explaining ageing through the application of reliability theory (Gavrilov and Gavrilova 2001) emerged, igniting the boom in mathematical modelling. These models departed from the physical interpretation of parameters in mathematical functions representing mortality rates and focused on appropriate mathematical modelling of physical characteristics in biological functions. In this regard, the mortality rate model in this study can be considered similar to the approaches presented in Gavrilov and Gavrilova (1991) and Gavrilov and Gavrilova (2001). Additionally, Penna (1995) gained significant attention by modelling the process of evolutionary ageing through the accumulation of mutations using numerical simulations and simultaneously explaining the exponential increase in mortality rates.
Strehler and Mildvan (1960) defined the concept of vitality and stated the following:

p.italic: An organism consists of a number of subsystems, each of which has a certain maximum ability to restore initial conditions after a challenge. Death occurs when the rate at which an organism does work to restore the original state is less than that demanded to overcome the effects of a given challenge.

sec.p: Their model directly modified the expression of the mortality rate based on this concept. In this study, we start by specifically modelling the subsystems themselves and defining the human individual as a collection of these subsystems. For each subsystem, we incorporate the ageing phenomenon by including a decline in the system’s functional level while maintaining a certain self-repair mechanism against externally occurring probabilistic shocks. We define the failure of a subsystem as the point at which the functional level falls below a certain threshold (denoted as 0 in this study) and relate it to the death of a human, which is an aggregate of subsystems.

The derivation of the time of subsystem failure is based on the first exit times in stochastic theory. Previous research using first exit time based on stochastic theory includes the work of Weitz and Fraser (2002), who assumed a random walk with drift as a probability variable that affects individual viability. In their model, these stochastic fluctuations can act in both directions, leading to a decrease or improvement in survival rates. In contrast, this study focuses on the human body’s functional level and treats shocks as probability variables that only occur in the negative direction, causing a decrease in the functional level. Furthermore, we introduce a certain self-repair mechanism that improves the functional level in the positive direction. This unique aspect distinguishes our study from previous research. Additionally, our study stands out from others as it excels in adopting a biological approach to mathematical modelling of the ageing process.

First, in Sect. 2, we provide an overview of the self-repair mechanisms of human biological functions and the hierarchical structure of tissues and organs that constitute a living organism. Next, in Sect. 3, we mathematically build the model based on the concepts introduced in Sect. 2. In Sect. 3.1, we define the number of survivors and the mortality rate. In Sect. 3.2, we model the functional level of the subsystems. We introduce external shocks as random variables and define the time when the functional level becomes zero, which corresponds to the time of failure. In Sect. 3.3, we derive the probability density function of the time of failure. The derivation employs the technique of Laplace transforms. By giving the physical interpretation of the image function after the Laplace transform, we solve the resulting differential equation and show the explicit expression of the probability density function of the time of failure. In Sect. 3.4, we discuss the moments of the time of failure, namely the mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis. This model is highly useful as it allows for the explicit determination of probability density functions and moment generating functions, enabling the analytical understanding of physical quantities such as the mean and variance and the evaluation of the dependencies of various parameters. In Sect. 3.5, we define the relationship between the failure of each subsystem and the death of a human. We derive the probability distribution function, probability density function, and expression of the mortality rate for the time of human death. In Sect. 4, we conduct a comparison between the observed survival curve and the survival curve derived from the model. In Sect. 4.1, we explain the rationale behind using the 2019 life tables for Japan and the UK to estimate the parameters of the ageing model. Section 4.2 outlines the methodology and specific procedures used to estimate the model‘s parameters. In Sect. 4.3, we present the results of the parameter estimation and, recognising that multiple combinations of parameters can fit the life tables, we refine the parameter ranges by assuming more realistic physical models of biological tissues and organs. In Sect. 4.4, we discuss the estimated values obtained, as well as compare the findings between Japan and the UK, and explore the relationship between human mortality and the failure of subsystems as inferred from the estimates. Finally, in Sect. 5, we summarise the paper and discuss potential extensions of the model in the future.

sec.title: Ageing and death as a decline in biological function
sec.p: Organisms undergo growth, maturation, ageing, and eventual death. Ageing progresses over time, ultimately culminating in an end of lifespan. Ageing and lifespan are intimately intertwined. Ageing can be described as a progressive deterioration of biological functions over time. As the functioning of tissues and organs within the body diminishes, it ultimately leads to the manifestation of mortality. Therefore, when constructing a mortality model, it is necessary to incorporate this decline in biological function. Living organisms are constantly exposed to stochastic external shocks, and in rare cases of significant shocks, their functional levels can drastically decrease. On the other hand, organisms possess a self-repair mechanism, which allows for restoration. For example, when skin is wounded, blood coagulates to seal the wound, and internal tissues regenerate over time, returning to a near-original state. Thus, the rate of functional decline, i.e., ageing, is believed to be determined by the interplay between the negative impact of external shocks and the positive influence of self-repair mechanisms.

In the case of human beings and other organisms, there exist hierarchical structures, including cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and individuals. Each subsystem at a particular level constitutes the subsystem of the higher level. Furthermore, while each subsystem functions independently, there are interactions between the subsystems within the same level, contributing to overall coordination. Therefore, the decline in the function of one subsystem can lead to the impairment of another subsystem. For example, renal dysfunction is known to increase the burden on the heart, leading to myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, respiratory failure (reduced lung function), and ultimately heart failure. Additionally, diseases such as diabetes, vasculitis, and sepsis can simultaneously cause the decline of multiple organ functions, such as the heart and kidneys. In the model construction presented in this study, we consider the human body as a collection of subsystems and discuss the functional decline of each subsystem. This framework ensures the characteristic sharp increase in human mortality rates in older age groups, as discussed in later sections. In the following section, we will provide a concrete representation of these physical phenomena using mathematical formulae.

sec.p: Figure 4 illustrates the trends in mortality rates by leading causes of death in Japan. In Japan, in 1950, the level of medical progress, healthcare technology, and convenience of medical facilities was not as high as compared to Western countries, and infectious diseases such as tuberculosis had a significant impact. Considering that Japan experienced the first lifespan transition later than many other advanced countries, the two different types of lifespan transitions mentioned earlier occurred simultaneously in the 1950 s and 1960 s (Horiuchi and Wilmoth 1998). As we moved into the 1970 s, lifestyle-related diseases became the dominant cause of death. Therefore, it is assumed that utilising the life tables of Japan and the UK for the year 2019 would be sufficiently effective for the parameter estimation of the mortality model.

sec.p: To begin with, regarding the total number of subsystems, n, we assumed a range of 100 to 1,000. This assumption is based on the fact that the total number of tissues and organs in a typical adult body is in the order of hundreds. Therefore, we will discuss the other parameters estimated under this assumption within this section.

sec.title: Differences in parameter levels between Japan and the UK
sec.p: Nevertheless, alongside the above considerations, we must also acknowledge the limitations of the model. The limitation is the simplicity of the model, such as the fact that parameters are time-independent. As a result, it would be premature to attribute regional differences in the frequency or size of external shocks solely to regional factors. In order to build a model capable of meaningfully comparing the parameter levels between Japan and the UK, a more complex model that incorporates other parameters to account for regional, temporal, and sex differences will be required.

In conclusion, from the perspective of comparing the parameter levels between Japan and the UK, we are not yet at a stage where it is meaningful to discuss the physical significance of these levels. The only insight that can be drawn from the comparison between the two countries is that the range of parameter sets obtained in each country is largely similar.

sec.title: Insights into subsystem derived from the parameter estimation
Conclusion and future extensions of the model
sec.p: In this study, inspired by the vitality model proposed by Strehler and Mildvan (1960), we constructed a model of human biological functions and incorporated the deterioration of functional levels as an ageing phenomenon, leading to a rational explanation of human survival and mortality rates. In the model construction, we considered the individual organism as a collection of subsystems and introduced a certain self-repair mechanism in the positive direction to counterbalance the negative external shocks that stochastically occur in each subsystem. We defined the failure of a subsystem when its functional level reached zero and defined the death of an individual, that is, a human when at least one subsystem fails. We explicitly derived the probability density function at the time of death using the inverse Laplace transform and demonstrated the existence of parameter sets that fit well with the observed survival curves using population demographic data from Japan and the UK. However, in estimating model parameters, there are multiple parameter sets that fit life tables with a certain accuracy. Therefore, by assuming a more realistic physical model of biological tissues and organs, we narrowed down the range of each parameter.
